rationale: B wins because it keeps the same real stories but has better claim discipline: "do not assert they lack it — let the reporter verify" is exactly the adult supervision this launch needs. A is often sharper, but it lets swagger outrun the file with lines like "Ramp can't copy quickly" and "distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer." Use B as the base and steal A's tougher uncomfortable questions.
gaps_in_A: "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" is not in the update. This is expenses, cards, reimbursement, enterprise requests, and venture-backed startups; payroll and mid-size are decorative imports.
"Ramp can't copy quickly" turns a competitive hypothesis into a claim. The facts say Brex competes with Ramp, not that Ramp lacks comparable coverage or faces a timing disadvantage.
"distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer" is invented trend scaffolding. Nothing supplied says remote work, Series B hiring, or global employment drove this launch.
"employees front costs on personal cards and wait on FX-mangled reimbursements" may be the right pain, but it needs a customer before it can be stated as reality.
gaps_in_B: "mostly been fought on features and pricing in the US" sounds plausible, but it is not in the update. Competitive-history claims need prior coverage or vendor proof.
"fintechs built for venture-backed startups move upmarket" overstates the arc. The update gives enterprise demand and venture-backed customers, not a proven upmarket migration story.
"means dozens of regulatory and banking arrangements" is a smart mechanics angle, but it is still an inference until Brex discloses licenses, partner banks, or market setup.
The next step is too thin: "pick the angle you can actually prove" is correct, but the set should force the country list and one named customer before any outreach.
